what_you_do: You write how you read a situation, look at it through three lenses, and sort the readings by how well they fit.

method.name: Reappraisal (cognitive reappraisal)
method.text: How we read a situation shapes how we feel about it. Reappraisal means looking for other realistic ways to read the same situation, not pretending it's fine. One lens asks what you'd say to a friend; taking a step back like this is called self-distancing. Another asks what will matter in a month; looking ahead like this is called temporal distancing.

research.text: A review of emotion-regulation experiments suggests that reconsidering what a situation means reduces negative feelings, with a small-to-moderate effect measured straight afterwards.
research.who: 306 experimental comparisons · settings to be confirmed from the full text

research.text: Research with 170 adults suggests reappraisal isn't always helpful: being good at it went with fewer depressive symptoms when stress was out of people's control, and with more when it was within their control. That's why this exercise asks whether you can do something about the situation.
Experiments suggest that talking about yourself from a distance, using your own name instead of “I”, can lower distress in stressful tasks.
Experiments suggest that picturing how a recent stressful event will look from the distant future can lower distress, partly because it draws attention to how temporary the event is.
research.who: 7 experiments from one research group · who took part to be confirmed from the full text

similar_note: No research has tested a short, self-guided exercise like this one with three lenses and a fit board.
about_this_exercise: This exercise uses reappraisal, but this version hasn't been tested itself. The research above used other instructions and measured feelings right afterwards.
limits: Changing how you see something doesn't change the situation. If you can act on it, planning a step may matter more.
The before-and-after ratings show how it feels right now, not whether the exercise works.
